item.description:
Model Context Protocol

What is MCP?

An open standard for connecting AI apps to the tools and data they use. A server says what it can do, the app shows that to the model, and when the model wants something the app calls the server and hands the result back.

Host the AI app you use: Claude, Cursor, ChatGPT, an agent Server a small program exposing tools, data or prompts Model decides what to use; never talks to a server directly Not REST JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout or one HTTP endpoint, and servers can talk back Not just JSON-RPC JSON-RPC is the envelope. MCP defines what goes in it: the methods, capability negotiation, transports and auth

item.title: September in Servo: <progress>, rounded rectangles, and more
item.description:
Servo 0.7.0 contains all of the changes we landed in September, spanning 527 commits!

The developer tools console now eagerly evaluates JS inputs, allowing faster feedback (@freyacodes, #47527).

We’ve shipped new web platform features:

the :checked pseudoclass (@skyz1, #47987) the user-select property (@SimonSapin, @mrobinson, #48137, #48242) the <progress> element (@rayguo17, #46974) CSS typed arithmetic (@Loirooriol, #48338) the alpha() CSS function (@Loirooriol, #48344) the font-width property (@Loirooriol, #47914)

Plus a bunch of new DOM APIs:

parentRule on CSSRule and CSSStyleDeclaration (@skyz1, #47743) version on HTMLHtmlElement (@SilvioPilato, #47786) getComposedRanges() and direction on Selection (@mrobinson, #47683) baseURL on CSSStyleSheet (@Gae24, #47783) CSS modules(@Gae24, #47813) and text modules (@Gae24, #47863) getContextAttributes() on CanvasRenderingContext2D and OffscreenCanvasRenderingContext2D (@Taym95, #47868) the Content-Language header (@TimvdLippe, #47930) dir on Document (@yezhizhen, #48170) SVGAElement, SVGPatternElement, SVGTSpanElement, SVGTextContentElement, SVGTextElement, SVGTextPositioningElement (@mu-mostafa98, #48174) the MLKEM768-X25519 algorithm for WebCrypto (@kkoyung, #48240, #48282, #48313, #48350) roundRect() on CanvasRenderingContext2D (@yezhizhen, #48293) paintTime and presentationTime on PerformancePaintTiming (@shubhamg13, #47926) getCueAsHTML() on VTTCue (@TimvdLippe, #48146) Security

We upgraded to SpiderMonkey v153.3 and mozangle v0.7, both of which included fixes for security bugs reported upstream (@sagudev, #48176, #47655, #48259).

Real world compat

The egui.rs demo now works as expected with --pref dom._webegpu_enabled.

This Candy Crush game is now playable.

We’re interested to hear how well your favourite websites run in Servo! Report successes in this Zulip thread or this Github discussion, and failures in our GitHub issues.

Work in progress

Our accessibility tree (--pref accessibility_enabled) now reports geometry bounds for inline elements (@alice, #47905) and does much less work when responding to DOM changes (@alice, @mrobinson, #47690). Additionally, elements with display: none are reported as hidden (@alice, #47772).

We had lots of conformance improvements for our WebGL2 implementation (--pref dom_webgl2_enabled) (@mxmgorin, #48423, #48441, #48470, #48479, #48495, #48473, #48536).

Support for WSIWYG editors (which rely heavily on contenteditable) is going very well: keyboard inputs are now hooked up when --pref dom_exec_command_enabled is present, so many editors are now usable (example).

Closed captioning for video elements is making progress. Text tracks now fire enter, exit, and cuechange events (@TimvdLippe, #47725). Media elements now return the full sorted list of text tracks (@TimvdLippe, #47785), and adding cues to a text track now sets that track correctly (@TimvdLippe, #48012). Text track objects now reflect the attributes of the associated <track> element. Text track URLs are fetched at the correct time (@TimvdLippe, #48325), and active cues are computed correctly (@TimvdLippe, #48305), while text track cues are ordered as expected (@TimvdLippe, #48368). Additionally, WebVTT parsing can now recover from errors (@TimvdLippe, #48391).

The Sanitizer API (--pref dom_sanitizer_enabled) now accepts the javascriptURLs property (@skyz1, #47867).

IndexedDB continues to improve: tables no longer error if unrelated tables contain duplicate index names (--pref dom_indexeddb_enabled) (@leowatts, #47936). Additionally, we implemented openCursor() and openKeyCursor() on IDBIndex (@kuntal-devrat, #48281), as well as advance(), continue(), and continuePrimaryKey() on IDBCursor (@kuntal-devrat, #48400).

We implemented the getTimeline() and setTimeline() methods for the Animation interface (--pref dom_web_animations_enabled) (@simonwuelker, #48122).

Embedding API

There’s a new API for events originating from accessibility tools: Servo::forward_accessibility_action (@alice, @mrobinson, #48512).

There is also an API to clear session history: WebView::clear_session_history (@Narfinger, #47483).

The WebView::set_throttled API has been removed (@mrobinson, #39923). Throttling automatically occurs when a WebView is hidden and is stopped when shown.

The WebViewDelegate::notify_focus_changed method was removed, along with the Servo methods focus and blur (@mrobinson, #48364). Embedders must call WebView::set_focused whenever a WebView has gained or lost system focus.

The webgl feature has been added to the default_web_features feature (@janeoa, #47866). If an embedding does not want to ship with WebGL support they will now need to disable default features.

Multiprocess mode is enabled at build time with the new Cargo feature multprocess (@Narfinger, #47360). To remove support for this feature (reducing binary size by ~2MB), build Servo with default features disabled.

Two new preferences exist to tune garbage collector behaviour: js_mem_gc_malloc_threshold_base_mb and js_mem_gc_urgent_threshold_mb (@mxmgorin, #47999). These can help on memory-constrained devices, and more information is available in the SpiderMonkey source (base, urgent).

The JVM compatibility target was raised to 11 on Android (@veyndan, #48414).

For users and developers

It is now possible to cross-compile the OpenHarmony build from Windows hosts (@jschwe, #48392).

Unhandled promise rejections are reported to the JS console (@TTyChud, #48486), making it easier to narrow down web compatibility issues in Servo.

The OpenHarmony SDK was updated to API level 23 (@Narfinger, #48505).

Pressing Control+A (or Command+A on macOS) now selects all the content in a document (@dzfrias, @mrobinson, #48025). It is no longer possible to copy text inside of password inputs (@dzfrias, #48404).

Embedder-originating JS (e.g. devtools console or embedding APIs) will always execute, even in documents that disable scripting via sandboxing or CSP (@derdilla, #48394).

Performance and stability

We improved performance by removing unnecessary allocations (@Narfinger, @TimvdLippe, @yezhizhen, #47689, #47839, #47838, #47982, #48006, #48036, #48099, #48204, #48127, #48218, #48357, #48386, #48422, #48440, #48452, #48508), preallocating more when building vectors (@jschwe, @Narfinger, @sagudev, @webbeef, #47455, #47613, #48026, #48398), and avoiding IPC in single process mode (@leowatts, @Narfinger, @Uiniel, @TTyChud, #47691, #47718, #48002, #48073, #48476, #48435).

We also sped up Servo by reducing interactions with the GC (@TimvdLippe, @Narfinger, #47818, #48257, #48396), and doing less work when modifying selections (@SimonSapin, #47579), dispatching events (@webbeef, #48078), calculating font metrics (@RichardTjokroutomo, #48238), and indexing window frames (@mrobinson, #47832).

We reduced memory usage in common cases by reusing buffers (@Narfinger, #47751), clearing more page-specific data (@Radeonares32, @Narfinger, @jschwe, @mrobinson, @mxmgorin, #47651, #47806, #47805, #48166, #48295, #48297, #48016), compacting data structures (@Narfinger, @webbeef, @SimonSapin, @mrobinson, #47776, #48039, #48050, #47742, #48301, #48296, #48105), and sharing more buffers (@jdm, #47998). We also fixed a memory leak involving <audio> and <video> elements (@TTyChud, #48371).

We turned on thread affinity boosting on Linux, which can improve performance on some CPU architectures (@jschwe, #47058).

We’re working on statically preventing a footgun that can lead to uncollectible GC cycles and leaking memory (@Gae24, @jdm, @lumiscosity, @SilvioPilato, @sahilnyk, @TTyChud, @kuntal-devrat, @MohamedAli00949, #47941, #48013, #48021, #48035, #48033, #48051, #48072, #48171, #48209, #48248, #48246, #48264, #48285, #48311, #48408, #48053, #48156, #48186, #48223, #48315, #47872, #47698, #47682, #47735, #47816, #47817, #47794, #47909, #47934, #47935, #47954, #48022, #47955, #48058, #48228, #48247, #48261, #48280, #48302, #48316, #48328, #48346, #48355, #48262, #48377, #48304, #48378, #48388, #48432).

We fixed panics in WebRTC (@MunishMummadi, #4772), execCommand() on Document (@TimvdLippe, #47784), <video> (@calvaris, #46148), <iframe> (@jdm, #48465), SharedWorker (@mrobinson, #47940), ancestorOrigins on Document (@mrobinson, #48009), about:memory (@mxmgorin, #47686, #48001), and EGL 1.4 configurations (@mxmgorin, #47803).

We also fixed a very ironic panic triggered by the about:crash page that loads when a normal page triggers a panic (@mrobinson, #48055)

The JS console no longer hangs when primitive values as thrown as exceptions (@FatCat560, #47629). Servo no longer hangs on shutdown in multiprocess mode (@Narfinger, #48523), when certain pages use IntersectionObserver (@mxmgorin, #47693), when closing a browsing context with pending WebDriver commands (@yezhizhen, #48131, #48172), or when closing SharedWorkers (@nicoburns, #48477).

about:memory got more improvements: we measure more memory for SVG rendering (@Narfinger, @mrobinson, #47061), WebAudio (@jdm, #47996), and identify globals that have been leaked (@jdm, #48237).

More on the web platform

CSS images now delay the load event, leading to more consistent behaviour for engine users performing visual rendering (@TimvdLippe, #48199).

Interactive selections in documents continued to improve! They now can span shadow trees (@mrobinson, @SimonSapin, #47931, #47694, #47895), and have consistent heights and positions (@mrobinson, #47937), plus there are new context menu entries to copy and select all (@mrobinson, #48101). Additionally, image-based content shows when it is part of a selection (@mrobinson, #48149).

Window.open() respects sandbox flags that prevent popups (@mrobinson, #47653).

LargestContentfulPaint now reports the loadTime for image content (@shubhamg13, #48286), ignores cross-origin frames (@shubhamg13, #48094), ignores invisible text (@shubhamg13, #48010), and reports null elements when they are removed from the tree (@shubhamg13, #48125).

select() on a text input now focuses the control (@dzfrias, @mrobinson, #48475).

Our WebDriver server now automates setting permissions (@xbwwj, @yezhizhen, #47623), while sending click events and keyboard actions uses fewer delays (@yezhizhen, #48066).

There are more useful error messages for methods on Document (@eachra-bawn, #47835) and CSS-related interfaces (@eachra-bawn, @jdm, #47746).

We upgraded our stylo dependency, which improves compatibility with contrast-color(), color-mix(), vertical-align, list-style, place-items, at-rule(), calc(), alpha(), attr(), content: attr(), and named-feature() (@Loirooriol, #46987, #47942).

We also fixed bugs related to visibilityState on Document (@yezhizhen, #47908), containsNode() on Selection (@mrobinson, #47938), setKeyframes on KeyframeEffect (@simonwuelker, #48103), selections when focusing a text input (@mrobinson, #48107), AudioParam clamping and automation (@kevlu93, #48351, #48347), PannerNode outputs (@kevlu93, #48510), the muted attribute on HTMLMediaElement (@TimvdLippe, #48403), placeholders in text inputs (@jdm, #47761, #47797), animations when modifying document stylesheets (@SharanRP, #48000), gradient color stops (@BudiArb, #48288), sticky table rows (@TTyChud, #48380), ::first-letter (@Loirooriol, #48307), text-wrap-mode (@mrobinson, #48469), OTF fonts (@wood-ghost, #47904), CSS and nosniff (@sahvx655-wq, #45481), Sec-Fetch- headers and redirects (@TimvdLippe, #48203), moveBefore() on Node (@mrobinson, #47692), supports() on WebCrypto (@kkoyung, #47768, #47891, #47953, #47984, #48410, #47545), cross-origin windows (@mrobinson, @jdm, #47632, #48411, #48038), origins of about:blank and about:srcdoc (@mrobinson, #47630), keypress events (@mrobinson, #48324), text and media documents (@SilvioPilato, #47823), body() on Response (@TTyChud, #48409), <details> with <summary> (@TimvdLippe, #48224), editing hidden inputs (@dzfrias, #48165), attribute nodes in XPath (@leowatts, @mrobinson, #47912), absolutely positioned boxes (@mxmgorin, #48081), CSS Grid containers with absolutely positioned nodes (@nicoburns, #47519), WebDriver wheel/pointer actions (@yezhizhen, #48143), and blob: URLs (@Gae24, #47910).

New contributors

A special thanks to the following people for landing their first patch in Servo:

Arnau Camprubí (@Arnau478, #47726) Silvio Pilato (@SilvioPilato, #47786) Radeonares32 (@Radeonares32, #47651) derdilla (@derdilla, #47828) pr3pony (@pr3pony, #48030) Mario (@Fatcat560, #47629) TtyChud (@TTyChud, #48228) Devrate Kuntal (@kuntal-devrat, #48247) Diego Frias (@dzfrias, #48025) LiamillionSS (@LiamillionSS, #48424)

Interested in helping build a web browser? Take a look at our curated list of issues that are good for new contributors!

Donations

Thanks again for your generous support! We are now receiving 8144 USD/month (+1% from August) in recurring donations. This helps us cover the cost of our speedy CI and benchmarking servers, one of our latest Outreachy interns, and funding maintainer work that helps more people contribute to Servo.

Servo is also on thanks.dev, and already 37 GitHub users (+1 from August) that depend on Servo are sponsoring us there. If you use Servo libraries like url, html5ever, selectors, or cssparser, signing up for thanks.dev could be a good way for you (or your employer) to give back to the community.

We now have sponsorship tiers that allow you or your organisation to donate to the Servo project with public acknowlegement of your support. If you’re interested in this kind of sponsorship, please contact us at [email protected].

Use of donations is decided transparently via the Technical Steering Committee’s public funding request process, and active proposals are tracked in servo/project#187. For more details, head to our Sponsorship page.

item.title: Alpine Linux Security Advisory: OpenSSH-server password authentication bypass
item.description:
Security advisory: openssh-server password authentication bypass

If you run sshd on Alpine Linux, update openssh now and restart sshd. Upgrading the package alone does not replace the running daemon.

If you cannot update yet, at least disable password logins: set PasswordAuthentication no in your sshd configuration and restart sshd. Either one closes the hole.

What is the problem?

An attacker who can reach your SSH port can log in without knowing any password. It takes one connection, works every time, and needs no retries.

The attacker needs the name of an account whose password field is * (an account with no password set, which is normal for key-only accounts), and needs the machine to have at least one other account with a $5$ or $6$ password hash. The attacker then sends a very long password (257 to 1024 bytes). One user with a password is enough: it makes every account without one reachable.

Details are in the OpenSSH 10.6p2 release notes. No CVE identifier had been assigned at the time of writing.

Who is affected?

You are affected if all of the following are true:

You run the Alpine openssh-server package, which is built without PAM, or you run openssh-server-pam with UsePAM no. (openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes is not affected.) PasswordAuthentication is yes (the OpenSSH default, unless you changed it). The machine has an account whose password field is *. This includes: root, which ships as root:* in the base image since about Alpine 3.16. OpenSSH’s default PermitRootLogin prohibit-password protects root, so root is only reachable if PermitRootLogin yes is set. That does not help if another account that can log in is able to become root, for example through doas.Any key-only user created with adduser without a password, or with usermod -p '*'.Users coming from a directory service through musl-nscd (nslcd, winbind, sssd), since they have no shadow entry.The alpine user in the official tiny-cloud images (see below). At least one local account has a $5$ or $6$ password hash.

Affected releases: every Alpine release we checked, 3.21 through 3.24 and edge, and the older releases that no longer receive regular updates (3.16 to 3.20).

Who is not affected? Docker and other container users that do not run sshd in the container. Systems with PasswordAuthentication no. Systems using openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes (with UsePAM no you are affected). Locked accounts: those with ! as the password field in /etc/shadow (a line starting user:!:). They cannot log in with a password or a key. Systems where no account has a $-style password hash. Cloud images configured through cloud-init, which writes PasswordAuthentication no. How can I fix it? 1. Update apk upgrade -U -a

Alpine 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8 and 3.24.4 contain the fixed package (see the release announcement). The fixed package versions are:

Branch Fixed openssh version edge 10.6_p2-r0 3.24 10.3_p1-r2 3.23 10.2_p1-r1 3.22 10.0_p1-r11 3.21 9.9_p2-r1 3.20 9.7_p1-r6 3.19 9.6_p1-r3 3.18 9.3_p2-r4 3.17 9.1_p1-r7 3.16 9.0_p1-r6

Restart sshd after upgrading (rc-service sshd restart). Upgrading the package does not restart a running sshd, so you must do it after.

2. If you cannot update: disable password authentication

Before you start, make sure your SSH key login works, and keep your current session open until you have tested a new login.

Run these as root. The first two commands create a drop-in file. Alpine’s default sshd_config reads that directory from 3.19 onward; older releases ignore it. The sed command changes yes to no on every PasswordAuthentication line in /etc/ssh/sshd_config, whatever the spacing, including lines inside a Match block. It also adds PasswordAuthentication no at the top of the file, for the case where there was no such line, and saves the original as /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak. The last two commands check the configuration, restart the daemon, and show the result:

mkdir -p /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d echo 'PasswordAuthentication no' > /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf sed -i.bak -e '1i PasswordAuthentication no' \ -e 's/^\(\s*PasswordAuthentication[^y#]*\)yes/\1no/i' \ /etc/ssh/sshd_config sshd -t && rc-service sshd restart sshd -T | grep -i passwordauthentication

The last command should print passwordauthentication no. To undo, delete /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-no-passwords.conf and copy /etc/ssh/sshd_config.bak back over /etc/ssh/sshd_config.

Cloud images (tiny-cloud)

The official tiny-cloud images (the qcow2, VHD and AMI artifacts) from 3.18.11 through 3.24.3 ship an alpine user with a * password field and passwordless doas. They are safe on first boot. They become exploitable as soon as any $6$ hash exists on the machine, for example when an admin sets a console password, or user-data adds a user with hashed_passwd. An attacker then gets a shell as alpine and can use doas to become root.

Images built from 3.21.10, 3.22.8, 3.23.8, 3.24.4 and later include the fixed package. Images from earlier point releases do not, so on every running instance, update openssh or disable password authentication.

Releases that are no longer supported (3.21 and older)

These releases have the same bug. 3.21 reached its end of support on 2026-11-01, but we have published fixed packages for each release all the way back to 3.16.

How do I know if I was attacked?

Look in /var/log/messages for sshd lines reading Accepted password for an account that has no password (alpine, root, or any key-only user). Review doas use and recently created users, files and authorized keys on exposed machines. If you cannot rule out a login, treat the machine as compromised.

How could this happen?

When sshd is built without PAM, it checks a password by hashing the attempt with crypt() (the C library function that turns a password into its stored hash) and comparing the result to the stored password field. For an account whose stored field is too short to contain a salt (the random prefix of a hash), sshd borrows the salt of another account.

musl’s crypt() returns the string * as an error indicator when the key is over 256 bytes long. * is also exactly what the stored field contains for every account with no password, so the “hash” matches and the login succeeds.

OpenSSH 10.6p2 avoids the problem in sshd. The stable-branch packages above carry a patch for the same problem.

Credits

Reported by ÃzgÃ¼n KÃ¼ltekin of Wakefield. Thanks to Damien Miller and Darren Tucker of the OpenSSH project for the fix and the 10.6p2 release, to Timo TerÃ¤s for help analyzing the issue, and to Natanael Copa, who built and uploaded the updated packages.

item.title: We can do better than line-buffered output
item.description:
nullprogram.com/blog/2026/11/05/

Buffered output typically comes in two flavors: fully buffered and line buffered. If output goes to a terminal then the implementation automatically selects line buffering, flushing its buffer when a line is completed so that it reaches the user immediately. Otherwise it fully buffers, holding output until the buffer is full or an explicit flush event at some arbitrary point in the future. Line buffering is a common bottleneck in non-interactive terminal applications such that it’s worth redirecting output to a file or pipe in order to avoid it. It doesn’t have to be this way. We can have our cake and eat it, too: promptly delivering lines to a terminal at fully-buffered speeds.

For example, Info-ZIP unzip prints file names as it extract them from an archive. This printout dominates extraction time of archives with many small files. Sometimes I run unzip without options, then my terminal floods with file names and I know that my extraction is bottlenecked. So I cancel and restart with -q (quiet) to avoid the bottleneck, because it’s faster to start over than wait. Conscious of this experience, I avoided the problem in tugz unzip without changing the user interface. You get a listing but you don’t have to pay for it.

$ unzip example.zip Archive: example.zip inflating: example.bmp inflating: example.svg inflating: example.txt

Consider this C program that prints three lines:

#include <stdio.h> int main() { puts("a\nb"); puts("c"); }

If we examine the writes with, say, strace:

$ strace -o log -e write ./a.out a b c

We might see (here glibc):

write(1, "a\n", 2) = 2 write(1, "b\n", 2) = 2 write(1, "c\n", 2) = 2

Yes, glibc takes line buffering quite literally, even splitting writes on a string. Some implementations are a little more sophisticated:

write(1, "a\nb\n", 2) = 4 write(1, "c\n", 2) = 2

CPython makes exactly those writes for this program:

import sys sys.stdout.write("a\nb\n") sys.stdout.write("c\n")

Its rule is to flush if its buffer contains a newline after appending the new output, with the consequence of possibly outputting partial lines. Building on the previous example:

enum { BUF_ERR = 1 << 0, BUF_LINE = 1 << 1, }; typedef struct { uint8_t *buf; ptrdiff_t cap; ptrdiff_t len; int fd; int flags; } Buf; bool os_write(int fd, void *, ptrdiff_t); void flush(Buf *b) { if (!(b->flags & BUF_ERR) && b->len) { if (!os_write(b->fd, b->buf, b->len)) { b->flags |= BUF_ERR; } b->len = 0; } }

Such line buffering might be achieved with a test-then-flush:

bool has_newline(Buf *b) { int r = 0; for (ptrdiff_t i = 0; i < b->len; i++) { r |= b->buf[i] == '\n'; } return r; } void append(Buf *b, uint8_t *src, ptrdiff_t len) { uint8_t *end = src + len; while (!(b->flags & BUF_ERR) && src<end) { ptrdiff_t left = end - src; ptrdiff_t avail = b->cap - b->len; ptrdiff_t amount = avail<left ? avail : left; memcpy(b->buf+b->len, src, amount); b->len += amount; src += amount; if (amount < left) { flush(b); // make room } } // test-then-flush if line buffered if ((b->flags & BUF_LINE) && has_newline(b)) { flush(b); } }

If we’ve got a bunch of lines to print and append them one after another into the buffer, that’s a lot of writes which could have been one.

Eat all the cake

Let’s think about our goal: If the output is a terminal then we don’t want to hold back lines indefinitely. That’s not the same as a write on every newline. There’s already a solution for the problem where we’re in a hurry to send out data, but the underlying, buffer-oblivious caller makes lots of small writes: Nagle’s algorithm.

That is, flush the buffer if it’s been idle a short time. We don’t actually care about newlines in particular. The catch is that it requires tweaking the interface. Add a deadline to the buffer:

typedef struct { int64_t deadline; // ... } Buf; int64_t os_monotonic_clock(); void deadline_flush(Buf *b) { if ((b->flags & BUF_LINE) && b->len) { int64_t now = os_monotonic_clock(); if (b->deadline && now>b->deadline) { flush(b); b->deadline = 0; } else { b->deadline = now + DEADLINE; } } }

Where DEADLINE is something appropriate for human perception, like 100ms or so. We could poke this concurrently in a thread, awoken via futex when data is written to the buffer. But better to poke it between short stints of work, which is how tugz works. For example (using my strings):

for (/* filename in filenames */) { Str pre = S(" inflating: "); Str suf = S("\n"); append(&stdout, pre.data, pre.len); append(&stdout, filename.data, filename.len); append(&stdout, suf.data, suf.len); while (/* not done inflating */) { // 1. inflate block // 2. write block deadline_flush(&stdout); } }

If it processes multiple files within the deadline, their names write out together. No threads. The behavior difference compared to traditional flush-on-newlines is imperceptible to a humans, aside from the fact their program runs faster. One more reason not to bother with crummy C stdio.

item.title: Show HN: Stroq – a local audit of what your coding agent did and why
item.description:
Stroq reads your own Claude Code and Codex sessions and shows how many commands came from text your agent read, and which keys left your machine.

An example: a made-up machine with made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Hoo is Stroq's owl. Your card shows your own sessions.

npx @stroq/cli

It reads your last 30 days of sessions, your key files and the folders your agent worked in; prints key names, never values; writes nothing but a small cache under ~/.stroq; and sends nothing. No account, no telemetry.

npx @stroq/cli a card of your own sessions, like the one above npx @stroq/cli init stop it next time: guard your agent npx @stroq/cli why why an action was stopped npx @stroq/cli attack watch Stroq stop 36 known attacks, in a sandbox npx @stroq/cli uninstall remove Stroq

Every moment on the card has a stroq show line that prints the evidence behind it (npx @stroq/cli show 1). stroq help --all lists the other commands. Needs Node.js 22 or newer. Apache-2.0.

Stroq is a local security platform for AI coding agents: Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI and others. Its hooks judge every tool call before it runs. They deny curl | sh and outbound calls that carry a known secret from your machine, and they ask you first when a command repeats text the agent read, naming that text. The console shows which agents actually ask Stroq, and every decision with its reason. Sessions you already had can be checked too, without installing anything.

npx @stroq/cli console # the console: a private page on 127.0.0.1 npx @stroq/cli replay --all # your Claude Code sessions of the last 30 days against the policy; no hooks needed npx @stroq/cli sent # did your agent pass your keys on? key names, never values npx @stroq/cli init # hook into your agent and guard the next session

A made-up machine: made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Nothing was executed.

Check: the card of

stroq, made by the same code. Each moment opens with its evidence, under it one line for each agent.

Live: recorded decisions as they happen. A row opens into its chain: what the agent read, what it did, the decision, the rule.

Agents: add or remove Stroq's hooks, with the exact file change shown first. When Stroq was last asked, and which of an agent's settings weaken it.

Skills & MCP: every skill and MCP server by agent: where it came from, what the rules matched in it, what changed since you last looked.

The fifth screen is Rules: try an action without running it, turn rules on with a preview and a test, the history with an undo, and the rules reference. Connected means Stroq's hooks are in the agent's settings, not that the agent calls them: Test hook and Live show that.

Screens from a build just before 0.30.0, reading a made-up machine: made-up sessions, keys and hosts. Nothing was executed.

npx @stroq/cli console # a private page on 127.0.0.1 npx @stroq/cli console --workspace /path/to/repo # the project it should look at

Open the whole link it prints: it carries a key that is new each time the console starts. The console reads what Stroq already records on this machine. It changes an agent's settings or Stroq's policy only after you confirm a preview of that change; checks you run are saved under ~/.stroq.

It listens only on 127.0.0.1, needs no account and has no telemetry. Nothing in it starts your agent: Test hook runs the hook once, offline. Adding hooks from the console needs macOS or Linux; on Windows use stroq init. Details and limits: console guide.

From a source checkout:

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile pnpm --dir console install --ignore-workspace --frozen-lockfile pnpm platform:build pnpm platform --workspace /path/to/repo

Output of the 0.29.0 CLI on a made-up Claude Code transcript of the same story; the path is shortened.

stroq replay reads the agent's own transcript, so it works on sessions from before Stroq was installed: which content the agent read, and which later actions came out of it. --all goes through every session of the last 30 days and says which to open. Nothing runs and nothing is sent; the verdicts are today's policy's, not a record of what happened at the time.

stroq sent compares your Claude Code, Codex CLI and Cursor sessions with the credentials on your machine and says where each key went: sent to another company, maybe sent, seen by the AI, used with its own service, or blocked before it ran. It prints names and sources, never values. Start with the session secret scan walkthrough (no session yet? try it with a made-up key).

What a stroq sent finding looks like

Made-up keys, the built CLI's output, trimmed:

stroq sent: did your AI agent pass your keys on? 6 of your 6 keys appear in your agent sessions: 2 sent to another company, 1 maybe sent, 1 seen by the AI, 1 used with its own service, 1 blocked before it ran. Checked 3 sessions (Claude Code 2, Codex 1), 2026-10-02 to 2026-10-19. Compared with 6 keys: ~/.aws/credentials, ~/.npmrc, ~/work/shop/.env, ~/work/api/.env. SENT TO ANOTHER COMPANY: rotate these today (2) 1. STRIPE_SECRET_KEY from ~/work/shop/.env went to collector.example, in a curl command when 2026-10-11 14:02 UTC · Claude Code · ~/work/shop do revoke it at https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys, then update ~/work/shop/.env SEEN BY THE AI: your agent's model saw these keys (1) 4. aws_secret_access_key from ~/.aws/credentials seen in the output of a Read of ~/.aws/credentials when 2026-10-02 09:42 UTC · Claude Code · ~/work/api note Not ruled out: 2 later commands in that session could reach the network. do your agent's model saw it; rotate it if that matters: https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam/home#/security_credentials Stroq names a send only when it sees the key in the command that sent it. A script, a file or a variable can carry a key out without showing it.

stroq attack runs 36 attacks, from public reports and synthetic cells, against your policy in a throwaway home: on 0.30.0, 15 are denied, 21 are asked about, 0 pass through.

Before each action. Native hooks for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot CLI, Windsurf and Antigravity, a plugin for OpenClaw, and a stdio MCP proxy. Supported outbound calls containing a known secret can be denied; provenance ties later actions to the tool output they repeat. A question about a value copied from text the agent read is asked once per session in Claude Code, unless the session has started something in the background. After the fact. replay and sent read local session records, including sessions from before Stroq was installed. Old, rotated or unknown values may be missed, and a key that did not show in a command may still have left in a script, a file or a variable. A local transcript match does not by itself prove delivery to a model provider. Local. No outbound network calls from the hooks; the hook of an older Task Lock run speaks only to its local parent controller. No telemetry. Limits. A hook sees only what the host sends it, and that differs by agent and version. Matching is text-level, so a command the model writes from scratch does not trace back to a source. It is a filter, not a sandbox. Read the integration limits before relying on a live hook. Guide: everything, section by section. The Stacks Project, Formalized in Lean
item.description:
Today, Axiom is releasing our Lean formalization of the entire Stacks Project, the roughly 7,500-page open-source reference that lays the foundations of modern algebraic geometry. Spanning some 16 million lines of code, it is the largest integrated, reusable library of formalized mathematics ever built.

With this release, the full mathematical development of the Stacks Project is available as a single, machine-checked library. Researchers and AI agents alike can import its definitions and theorems directly into new formal proofs, while permanent Stacks tags link every Lean declaration back to the canonical text mathematicians already know.

This milestone begins with the Stacks Project itself. Initiated by Columbia University mathematician Johan de Jong in 2005, it has grown through the tireless work of hundreds of mathematicians who have contributed proofs, examples, and refinements over two decades. Our formalization rests equally on the foundations of the Lean and Mathlib communities. Formalizing a corpus of this magnitude was only possible because those communities spent years building a rich mathematical library, along with the abstractions needed to organize it, long before our work began.

Why formalize a foundational reference of this scale? As AI systems begin generating mathematical arguments at a pace far beyond what humans can inspect by hand, formal verification becomes essential. In fields with mature Lean infrastructure, new results can often be formalized shortly after they are discovered. Until now, modern algebraic geometry has been far harder to approach this way: a single contemporary proof may invoke a long chain of theorems across commutative algebra, schemes, sheaves, cohomology, and algebraic stacks before its core argument even begins. The mathematics existed in the Stacks Project, but the corresponding Lean infrastructure did not.

Closing that gap is as much a software engineering challenge as a mathematical one. While uncoordinated AI code generation can produce short, isolated scripts quickly, scaling to millions of lines of verified mathematics requires clean abstractions, stable interfaces, and components that fit together across an entire codebase. To achieve this, we deployed coordinated swarms of AI agents capable of translating, proving, and integrating thousands of theorems in parallel. Formalizing the Stacks Project in its entirety establishes a new starting point for algebraic geometry and the many neighboring fields that rely on its machinery.

The mathematics behind Stacks

At its heart, algebraic geometry studies the interplay between algebraic equations and the geometric shapes they describe. Over the real numbers, the equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1$ defines a circle; over the rational numbers, its points correspond to Pythagorean triples, such as $3^2 + 4^2 = 5^2$. Studying the same equations across different number systems, or in families that vary over a parameter space, connects geometry directly to number theory and algebra. These ideas also reach beyond pure mathematics: elliptic curves secure modern digital cryptography, while algebraic curves over finite fields power error-correcting codes. Modern algebraic geometry provides a common language for studying equations across all of these settings.

Forging that language took generations. Emmy Noether revolutionized algebra by shifting focus from individual equations to abstract structures such as rings, modules, and ideals. Just as the right software abstraction can replace thousands of special-purpose routines with a single reusable framework, a theorem proved for the right algebraic structure applies across many concrete settings at once. A generation later, Alexander Grothendieck and his collaborators introduced the theory of schemes, creating a sweeping dictionary between algebra and geometry that allowed mathematicians to do geometry over arbitrary rings, with arithmetic and infinitesimal data built in from the start. Monumental treatises like Éléments de géométrie algébrique (EGA) and Séminaire de géométrie algébrique du Bois Marie (SGA) rebuilt the foundations of the discipline from the ground up, supplying the machinery behind landmark breakthroughs including Deligne’s proof of the Weil conjectures and Wiles’s proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem.

Yet as the subject expanded, its foundational literature grew vast, scattered across thousands of pages of dense monographs and seminars, much of it written in French. A great deal of the subject's working knowledge also lived as unwritten folklore passed down from advisor to student. Even defining an algebraic stack, a geometric space capable of remembering the internal symmetries of the objects it parametrizes, requires a formidable tower of prerequisites spanning commutative algebra, topologies, sheaves, and cohomology. Mathematicians needed a unified, self-contained reference where those prerequisites were written down in full detail.

In 2005, de Jong set out to organize those foundations the way software engineers maintain an open-source project like the Linux kernel. What began as an accessible introduction to algebraic stacks evolved into a living, collaborative encyclopedia comprising thousands of permanent four-character tags. The Stacks Project operates on rigorous editorial principles: every theorem carries a proof, every assumption is stated explicitly, and every step points back to the exact tags on which it depends. In doing so, de Jong and his collaborators anticipated the architecture of formal proof libraries, demonstrating that mathematics becomes far easier to verify and extend when its components have stable identifiers and explicit dependency graphs. Translating the Stacks Project into Lean brings mechanical verification to that human-designed architecture.

A library built for reuse

On October 27, 2026, Axiom released our Lean formalization of the Classification of Finite Simple Groups (CFSG). While CFSG and the Stacks Project are both monumental in scale, they represent fundamentally different engineering challenges. CFSG is organized around a single landmark theorem. The Stacks Project, by contrast, is a foundational library: its value lies in thousands of interlocking definitions, constructions, and lemmas designed to be reused across countless future proofs.

With this library, a mathematician or AI agent formalizing a new theorem about families of curves no longer needs to reconstruct the foundations of schemes or coherent cohomology from scratch. They can import the relevant definitions and theorems directly, while Lean’s kernel guarantees that every cited result is applied only when its exact hypotheses are satisfied. Formalizing the Stacks Project as one connected codebase gives researchers and agents a common chain of verified definitions and theorems on which to build, something no collection of isolated proof scripts can provide.

To make our library easy to navigate, our release preserves the permanent tag structure of the original text. At stacks.axiommath.ai, readers can view the pages of the original Stacks Project side-by-side with the corresponding Lean code and explore the interactive dependency graph. Because a single Stacks tag often unfolds into multiple formal definitions and lemmas, some newly defined and others bridged directly to existing declarations in Mathlib, our interface tracks these mappings explicitly so researchers can see precisely how the informal and formal developments align.

Engineering coherent mathematics at scale

A smorgasbord of independently verified proofs does not make a usable mathematical library. If thousands of AI agents formalize theorems in parallel without architectural coordination, two agents will inevitably prove correct theorems about the same mathematical object using subtly incompatible definitions, or duplicate foundational infrastructure that already exists in Mathlib. Lean’s kernel will accept both files in isolation, but their results will be painfully difficult to compose downstream. Building coherent formal infrastructure requires keeping every definition and interface aligned across the entire project.

At this scale, formalization is as much systems engineering as it is mathematics. To build a single, unified library, our mathematicians and engineers designed a hierarchical system of AI agents with specialized responsibilities and strict coordination protocols. Agents worked in parallel across the dependency graph to translate statements, search Mathlib for existing abstractions, construct proofs, and resolve prerequisites, all while keeping definitions, typeclass interfaces, and mathematical abstractions aligned across chapters.

In a tightly interconnected dependency graph of definitions and theorems, an unfaithful or trivialized formalization is quickly exposed. Ensuring that each formal statement faithfully captures the mathematical meaning of the original text is even more important than verifying its proof. Across the library, statement faithfulness is enforced automatically at scale through multi-agent auditing, semantic cross-checks against the source text, and the strict requirement that every definition and lemma must successfully interface with the downstream theorems that depend on it. Combined with targeted audits on foundational definitions and landmark theorems, this automated verification pipeline ensures that the formal library remains faithful to the mathematics of the Stacks Project.

What formal verification reveals

Over the course of the project, our system surfaced dozens of statements in the Stacks Project that required local refinement, including missing hypotheses, edge cases in positive characteristic, and claims that did not hold in the full generality stated. Rather than treating failed proof attempts as mere obstacles, our agents diagnosed the underlying mathematical obstructions and constructed explicit counterexamples to prove where the original statements broke down.

Once an obstruction was isolated, the system worked to repair the mathematics so downstream chapters could still depend on it. For local oversights, our agents identified the exact missing hypotheses and formalized the corrected theorems alongside their counterexamples. Where a false supporting lemma created a gap in the proof of a deeper theorem, the agents found alternative routes through the literature to establish the main result under its original hypotheses. Together, these resolutions show how large-scale formalization can actively refine and strengthen the mathematical literature itself.

A monument to the past, a foundation for the future

Ultimately, the mathematics inside this library is the product of generations of human creativity, from the geometric intuition of the early pioneers, to the structural revolutions of Noether and Grothendieck, to the open-source scholarship of the Stacks Project and Mathlib communities. Each generation inherited a body of mathematical knowledge, cast it into a sharper language, and handed the next generation a stronger foundation. We see this formalization as part of that ongoing tradition: both a tribute to the mathematicians who built modern algebraic geometry, and working infrastructure for an emerging era in which humans and AI agents explore new mathematical frontiers together.

In an October 21, 2026 announcement, de Jong requested that AI-generated comments and pull requests not be submitted directly to the upstream Stacks Project repository for the time being. The Stacks Project remains an active, living text under the stewardship of Johan de Jong and its community of contributors, while this Lean formalization is an independent open-source project maintained by Axiom. We fully respect that boundary: we keep our formalization, counterexamples, and refinements in our own repository, where mathematicians can review and draw upon them on their own terms.

You can explore the side-by-side text, inspect counterexamples, and trace the full dependency graph at stacks.axiommath.ai. Like the Stacks Project itself, our formalization is open source and designed to grow over time. We invite mathematicians, Lean developers, and AI agents to examine the library, refine its abstractions, and build new mathematics upon it.

item.title: Window Sweaters
item.description:
A little Mac app I made to give my windows sweaters. 🧶 Knitted borders, colours inspired by your favourite apps, and a cosier desktop.

window-sweaters-demo-github.mp4

See Window Sweaters in action on X →

You can just send this repo to your coding agent and ask it to install Window Sweaters for you:

Install Window Sweaters on my Mac: https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters

Or install it yourself with Homebrew:

brew trust saragordic/tap brew install --cask saragordic/tap/window-sweaters

Then open Window Sweaters from your Applications folder.

You can also grab the latest ZIP from Releases, unzip it, and drag Window Sweaters.app into Applications.

If macOS blocks it, open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Open Anyway after trying to launch it. The app isn't notarized by Apple yet. Apple's instructions explain this step.

Click the yarn icon in your menu bar to change the style, pattern, border width, and stitch size. You can also pause the sweaters or quit from there.

To leave an app bare, open Apps and untick it. Its windows lose their sweater straight away, everything else stays as it is, and it stays off until you tick it again, even after a restart. Only want sweaters on a few apps? Choose Turn Off for All Apps, then tick the ones you like. Apps you open later start off too.

By App gives each app its own sweater. Zigzag gives them all a softer, matching cream zigzag in colours taken from their icons. Try both and see what you like.

If macOS asks for Accessibility access, enable Window Sweaters in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility so it can follow which window is focused.

Custom sweaters for 37 apps, and counting! Almost 40 little colourways, with colours picked by hand. These are just a few of my favourites:

Shown above in By App and Zigzag. Here’s everyone we’ve knitted for so far:

Apple: Finder, Safari, Mail, Messages, Notes, Calendar, Reminders, Apple Music, Photos, Preview, Terminal. Work and notes: Notion, Paper, Granola, Microsoft Teams, Slack, Zoom. Coding and AI: Cursor, VS Code, Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, Grok Bot, Ghostty. Design: Figma, Adobe Photoshop, Adobe Illustrator. Microsoft Office: Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook. More favourites: Spotify, WhatsApp, Google Chrome, Firefox, Telegram, Discord.

See every sweater and its close-up stitches in the catalogue, or download the By App PDF.

The 37 custom sweaters keep their hand-picked colours and patterns. Other apps borrow colours from their own icons, softened into yarn, and get a two-colour zigzag, picnic or twinkle sweater in By App mode. The pattern stays the same for each app. If an icon has no usable colour, the app keeps a stable colour chosen from its name.

Icons are sampled locally in the background when needed. While the colour is being prepared, the border uses its usual fallback. Zigzag uses icon colours for every app, the 37 custom ones included, with a cream zigzag, or a deeper shade of the app’s colour on pale apps. Colours you set in apps.conf always win. Other shared patterns keep their own contrast yarns, with each app’s own base colour.

I built this on my Mac and use it myself, but there are still rough edges. Borders hide while you resize a window and return when you're done.

The app is built for macOS 13 or later, on Apple Silicon and Intel. I've tested it on Apple Silicon with macOS 26; older macOS versions and Intel Macs haven't had the same hands-on testing. It uses private macOS window APIs, so system updates may affect how it works.

If something looks wrong, open an issue and tell me your macOS version, Mac model, and whether you're using another screen. Reproduction steps help a lot.

You'll need Apple's Command Line Tools (xcode-select --install) and Python 3.

git clone https://github.com/saragordic/window-sweaters.git cd window-sweaters ./scripts/build-app.sh python3 scripts/install-local.py

This builds outputs/Window Sweaters.app, installs it in ~/Applications, and opens it. The installer backs up any previous local installation before replacing it.

If you'd like to experiment, edit these files and restart the app:

~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/apps.conf ~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders/charts/

The folder still uses the app's original name so existing settings keep working. For example, an app rule looks like this:

Claude = #D58561 atelier-claude

Names match app-name prefixes, ignoring capitalisation; the longest match wins. You can also put your own PNG charts in the charts folder to replace built-in patterns.

If you like setting things up from the command line, Window Sweaters also runs an optional shell script at startup, if you have one at ~/.config/window-sweaters/sweatersrc or ~/.sweatersrc.

Quit Window Sweaters from the yarn icon first. Then, if you installed it with Homebrew:

brew uninstall --zap --cask window-sweaters

--zap also removes your saved colourways. Leave it off to keep them for later.

If you installed it by hand, drag Window Sweaters.app to the Trash, then delete these if you want everything gone:

~/Library/Application Support/Knit Borders ~/Library/Preferences/local.knitborders.app.plist

macOS remembers the Accessibility permission separately, so remove Window Sweaters from System Settings → Privacy & Security → Accessibility too.

make test # run the tests make catalogue # render the sweater collection make bench # benchmark the renderer

See CONTRIBUTING.md for more details.

item.title: Launch HN: Rivet (YC W23) – Scale and Orchestrate Agents on S3
item.description:
4.99 ms p99 cold starts, 72 KB RAM per Actor, scales to billions

Quickstart • Documentation • Changelog • Discord • X

Rivet is an orchestrator for agentic workloads built on the actor model. Each Rivet Actor is a long-lived process with in-memory state, a SQLite database, WebSockets for realtime, and scheduling, addressed by key. Create one per agent, session, user, or tenant, and run it on plain Node.js, Bun, or Rust.

72 KB per Actor: Actors share a node process instead of each booting a sandbox, so one server holds hundreds of thousands. 4.99 ms p99 cold starts: No image pull and no VM boot. SQLite backed by S3, at SSD speeds: 1.07 ms durable writes and 1.36 ms reads at p99, for about 10.4× less than replicated SSD storage. Hibernates when idle: Idle Actors cost nothing and wake on the next request with nothing lost.

Backend

import { actor } from "rivetkit"; import { db } from "rivetkit/db"; const agent = actor({ // Per-Actor SQLite database, persisted across restarts and hibernation db: db({ onMigrate: async (db) => { // Apply the SQLite schema await db.execute(`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (role TEXT, content TEXT)`); }, }), actions: { chat: async (c, text: string) => { // Durably save the message await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "user", text); const messages = await c.db.execute("SELECT role, content FROM messages"); const response = streamText({ model: openai("gpt-5"), messages }); // Stream tokens to every connected client for multiplayer for await (const delta of response.textStream) { c.broadcast("token", delta); } // Durably save the response await c.db.execute("INSERT INTO messages VALUES (?, ?)", "assistant", await response.text); }, }, });

Client (frontend or backend)

// Connect to an Actor const agent = client.agent.getOrCreate("agent-123").connect(); // Listen for realtime events agent.on("token", delta => process.stdout.write(delta)); // Call an action on the Actor await agent.chat("how many r's in strawberry?");

Paste this prompt into Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, or any coding agent:

Run npx skills add rivet-dev/skills, then ask me what to build and run it locally.

Every product Rivet ships is an Actor, scheduled by the same control plane.

Actors: Long-lived processes with state, realtime, and scheduling built in. Agents: A durable process per agent, with memory that survives restarts. Workflows: Multi-step operations that replay instead of starting over. agentOS: Run the code your agent writes, securely, with granular control over network access, filesystem access, and resource limits. Dynamic Apps (preview): A backend per user, deployed the moment it is generated. Coding agents: One Actor per agent, with a durable process and state that survives restarts. Agent app builders: Each generated backend deploys as its own Actor that scales to zero. Agents in your VPC: Run agents next to your databases and APIs, so no data leaves your cloud. Realtime apps: One Actor per document, room, or channel, broadcasting changes to every client. Metric Rivet Actor Sandbox Cold start (p99) 4.99 ms 1.70 s Memory per instance 72.4 KB 512 MiB Storage SQLite on S3 Disk per sandbox Storage cost 10.4× cheaper Replicated SSDs
Benchmark details & methodology Rivet numbers come from the published Rivet Actors vs Cloudflare Durable Objects benchmark, run on Rivet 3.0.3. Its repository has the raw samples and the scripts to reproduce them. Sandbox numbers are a documented default memory allocation and a third-party cold start benchmark. Storage cost compares S3 Standard with three Amazon EBS gp3 copies at AWS list prices. Sources, dates, and the full method are at rivet.dev/docs/benchmarking. Fault tolerance: If a node goes down, its Actors move elsewhere with their state intact. HTTP & WebSocket networking: Call an Actor over HTTP or hold a live WebSocket to it. End-to-end type safety: Typed clients for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. Cron & scheduling: Wake an Actor on a schedule or at a time it sets for itself. Actor-to-Actor calls: Actors call each other by key across the cluster. OpenTelemetry: Traces, metrics, and logs in OTel format. Option Description Get started Local & self-host Run Rivet locally while you build. In production, run the control plane on Docker, Kubernetes, or a VM. S3 is the only dependency. Self-hosting docs Rivet Cloud Fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. Run your nodes on Rivet Cloud or bring your own. Dashboard BYOC The control plane runs inside your own VPC on AWS, GCP, or Azure, fully managed by Rivet. Your data never leaves your cloud. BYOC docs

Every option runs the same control plane, from local dev to production. Talk to an engineer →

Typed SDKs for your backend and React hooks for your frontend. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun with no custom runtime, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.

Deploy nodes on: Docker Compose • Kubernetes • VM & bare metal • Hetzner • AWS ECS • Railway • Render

Runtimes: Node.js • Bun • Rust

Tools: Vitest • OpenTelemetry • Pino • AI SDK • OpenAPI • AsyncAPI

Does Rivet have BYOC?

Yes. Rivet deploys into your own cloud account, including air-gapped environments: the control plane and storage run inside your VPC while Rivet operates them. See the BYOC docs.

Does Rivet have a cloud?

Yes. Rivet Cloud runs fully managed, dedicated clusters on AWS or GCP in any region. It can run your app's Docker image as nodes on Rivet Cloud, or you can bring your own nodes.

Can I self-host Rivet?

Yes. Rivet is fully self-hostable; see the self-hosting docs. The control plane runs anywhere a container runs, with guides for Docker Compose, Kubernetes, VMs and bare metal, Hetzner, Railway, Render, and AWS ECS. For enterprise support with a self-hosted deployment, contact us.

Do I still need Postgres, FoundationDB, or NATS?

No. An object storage bucket is the only dependency: there is no database to run and no message bus, and control plane instances find each other through the bucket. Rivet works with Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, and any S3-compatible store such as MinIO, Cloudflare R2, or Hetzner Object Storage. A local filesystem backend is available for trying Rivet on one machine.

Is Rivet open-source?

Yes. Rivet is open source under the permissive Apache 2.0 license. You're looking at it.

How does Rivet compare to sandboxes?

A sandbox boots a VM or container per agent, which is slow to start and sits mostly idle. A Rivet Actor runs inside a shared node process: 72 KB and 4.99 ms p99 to start, versus 512 MiB and 1.70 s for a sandbox, and it hibernates when idle. To run untrusted code your agent writes, use agentOS.

How does Rivet compare to Cloudflare Durable Objects?

Rivet is often used as an open-source alternative to Cloudflare Durable Objects that is easy to self-host and scales. It also fixes many of the constraints of Durable Objects: no 128 MB memory cap, bottomless storage instead of a 10 GB SQLite limit, Actors are not randomly evicted, and you control the runtime because Actors run on vanilla Node.js or Bun instead of a custom runtime. Rivet also adds built-in connection handling, event broadcasting, durable scheduling and cron, full Vitest support, lifecycle hooks for draining, and control over Actor upgrades. See the Cloudflare Durable Objects comparison.

Does Rivet use a custom V8 runtime?

No. Rivet runs on native Node.js and Bun, so your existing packages, tooling, and tests work unchanged.

Is Rivet like Erlang, Akka, or Orleans?

Rivet implements the virtual actor pattern, which is closest to Orleans, but focuses on what modern workloads need: SQLite persistence instead of simple JSON stores and support for modern runtimes. Erlang and Akka do not provide virtual actors out of the box, though ecosystem packages exist that offer functionality comparable to Rivet Actors.

Does Rivet require microVMs, gVisor, or nested virtualization?

No. Rivet only needs a standard process that connects to the control plane over WebSocket. That process can be Node.js, Bun, Rust, or anything else.

item.title: The Hackintosh Reborn
item.description:
The Hackintosh Reborn... with AI

Almost a decade ago, I released a hackintosh guide on running macOS 10.14 through a VM with an x86 host. A "Hackintosh" is the feat of running macOS on non-Apple hardware, and has a history dating back to the late 1980s. At the time KVM and PCI passthrough were relatively new technologies, and this guide provided near-native performance with GPU acceleration.

A few years passed by, and we saw Apple release the first ARM-based Mac in 2021, the M1 MacBook Air. The timing was impeccable, Intel was unable to create competitive processors (due to being stuck on the 14nm node), and Apple had powerful and efficient ARM chips already being shipped in their iPhones. The long battery life, the fanless design, the instant wake, what's not to like? The benefits of switching to ARM were clear, however to most, this was thought to be the final chapter in the hackintosh community. x86 versions of macOS would soon be discontinued, and the hackintosh community would slowly fade away. That day has come and the latest version of macOS 27 (Golden Gate) released this year is no longer compatible with x86...

Just a few days ago, I decided to create an iOS app for the first time. It required XCode 26 for development, so I used my spare ThinkPad T490 as my development machine and installed macOS 26 using a posted guide. The installation was smooth and painless. XCode 26 has integrations with Claude Code and OpenAI Codex, and this was my first foray into AI-assisted coding. After some initial tinkering with x86 workarounds, I was pleased that I had a functional iOS app within a day, without touching a single line of code!

So how does this all tie in? Well, this is exactly what the Hackintosh community could hardly envision five years ago: the rise of AI. Waiting patiently and gently until now, the hackintosh and the hackios community has seen an absolute explosion in development, activity, and success in the past few weeks! As one person aptly wrote, this is the power of Claude Code with Ghidra on steroids. Just to list a few recent developments, we have:

macOS 27 running on the Snapdragon Laptop:

macOS 27.2 Beta on an ARM SBC RK3588 with Mali drivers:

iOS 17 running on the Nintendo Switch OLED:

Support for 50-series Nvidia GPUs with nullmoth:

I'm barely scratching the surface, with further developments in AirDrop, accelerated video decode, and even running translated macOS 27 on x86. As much as we lament the cost of AI, there are some glimmers of hope: you just might be able to have your hardware and own it too.

item.title: Hungary: Communist-era files released, up to 60k former agents revealed
item.description:
Hungary released communist-era secret police files Wednesday, identifying up to 60,000 informants, a path for Hungary in reckoning with its repressive past.

In spite of Hungary's democratic transition in 1990, efforts to disclose communist-era archives have repeatedly failed, with critics blaming successive governments' reluctance to implicate public figures across the political spectrum.

Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar ended this stall with a bill in September to grant unrestricted access for the public to the records for the first time.

"After 36 years, we are finally fulfilling what was once one of the key promises of the 1990 regime change — a promise that was later denied and lied about," Magyar told a media briefing at the state security archives.

"For decades, restrictions on public access provided opportunities for political hysteria, blackmail, the exertion of pressure, and silencing," he said.

Public figures featured in registry

Politicians, clergy members and TV personalities' names appeared in the registries. But a "large proportion" of the informants were "people who did not make their mark on national public life," said Bendeguz Gergo Cseh, the head of the archive.

The government will set up hotlines offering emotional support and counselling for those affected by the revelations.

"Following today's disclosure, a great many families will be confronted with information that is difficult for them to bear," Magyar said, asking people to treat the disclosure with "dignity and humanity."

Various types of documents disclosed

Under the law on the full disclosure of the previous regime’s secret service activities, four types of state security records dating from before 1990 will be made freely accessible to anyone.

On Wednesday morning, the three of these became accessible on the nyitottaktak.hu (source in Hungarian) website.

The "6 card" is the registration sheet for a network member. It contains the agent’s identifying data, including name, place and date of birth, mother’s name and occupation, but also the main details of the agent’s activity. Among them, the circumstances and motivations that led to them becoming an agent and how long they remained a network member.

A register of recruitment between 1957 and 1962 and a database of former agents' personal data and code names were also released. In total, estimates suggest 50,000 to 60,000 agent names were made public over all this document disclosure.

The public has free access since Wednesday to this data via a search tool that can filter by birth data, by name, place and date of birth, as well as by code name, across all types of records that have been made public.

A second batch of files with further detail on about 9,000 informants will be released in February.

Around 150,000 agents during communist era

Hungary was under one-party communist rule between 1949 and 1989 that repressed dissent.

Much like in East Germany and other parts of the Soviet-led Eastern Bloc during the Cold War, authorities employed an extensive network of informants to monitor public sentiment.

Individuals, often recruited through coercion, were tasked with reporting on colleagues, friends and even relatives for signs of disloyalty towards the regime.

Estimates suggest that secret police employed around 150,000 agents in total over the four decades of the Mátyás Rákosi (1952-1953) and János Kádár (1956-1988) regimes.

But only about one-third of their names are known, and detailed, substantive information exists for only about 10% of them. Many records were lost in 1956 and during the anti-Soviet change of regime, and the remainder was kept until 1997 in the Ministry of Interior, until the creation of ÁBTL’s predecessor, the Historical Office.

Cseh Gergő Bendegúz, director general of the Historical Archives of State Security Services (ÁBTL), told the Hungarian press agency MTI that there are about ten thousand files, comprising many hundreds of thousands of pages in total.

Responding to a question on how reliable and complete the documents are, Cseh Gergő Bendegúz underlined that the content of state security records is not necessarily true in every case and is certainly very incomplete.

'Better late than never'

Debates over opening the archives have dogged Hungarian politics since the fall of communism. In 2002, weeks after becoming prime minister, socialist politician Peter Medgyessy became embroiled in a scandal after it was revealed that he had worked as a communist-era secret agent.

The case prompted fresh calls for transparency, and parliament adopted a law in 2003 that allowed individuals who had been monitored to learn who had reported on them.

The release was "better late than never," said historian Laszlo Eorsi from the 1956 Institute Foundation.

"We are getting access to much more information than before about who the authorities have recruited and how the security apparatus worked back then," he said.

But historians have cautioned against judging anyone just because their names are on the list of informants.

"I know of quite a few examples when someone was recruited, but they did not make a report, but in fact took a huge risk by turning against the authorities. Some even could be considered proper heroes," Eorsi stressed.

item.title: Introducing Pangram Image 1.0
item.description:
Introducing Pangram Image 1.0

State-of-the-art AI image and video detection with our latest Pangram Image models.

Introducing Pangram Image 1.0 and Pangram Image Flash 1.0

A real photograph containing an AI image. Pangram Image 1.0 is able to locate the AI content with its heatmap.

A few months ago, we released Pangram Image as a research preview. We are now proud to announce Pangram Image 1.0: The state-of-the-art in both AI image and AI video detection. We would like to thank the whole community for taking the time to try it and find its weaknesses, and for holding us to a high standard to make a better detector for everyone.

What’s new Our new flagship AI image detection model, Pangram Image 1.0, with: State-of-the-art performance at detecting frontier AI image generatorsHeatmap output for localizing exactly where AI appears in imagesRobustness to edits, compression, and low resolutions A smaller, faster model, Pangram Image Flash 1.0, with: State-of-the-art performance at detecting frontier AI video generatorsFrame by frame analysis of AI edited videos Chrome Extension support for detecting AI in your feed API support for image and video Try it here Pangram Image 1.0 Frontier Image Detection

We tested our Pangram Image 1.0 model against several commercial and academic AI image detectors. We created synthetic mirrors of 100 real photos using 12 frontier state of the art AI image generators, using prompts that closely matched the original photo for a total of 1,200 synthetic images. Our model achieves 99.96% accuracy on this evaluation set.

Academic AI Image Detection Benchmarks

We are committed to providing the highest quality detection to our users. To test our model robustly, we compared it against several academic benchmarks for AI image detection.

Sources: X-AIGD · Mirage-Test · AIGenImages2026 · Synthbuster + RAISE comparison · Community Forensics

Robustness

Many social media platforms compress and downscale images, and malicious actors can also add blur, noise, and other artifacts to try to trick AI detectors into thinking AI images are real. We specifically train to detect these kinds of transformations, and we have found our model to be robust to these edits.

Low Resolution Detection

Our initial release limited image input to the minimum size of 512x512, as our accuracy dropped off at lower resolutions. We are now lowering this limit to 256x256, as we find our new model has improved accuracy at lower resolutions. At resolutions below 512, image detection results will come with a reduced confidence disclaimer.

Video Detection Pangram Image Flash 1.0

A recent academic study, DF26, showed that humans are barely better than random when it comes to telling real videos from AI videos of people talking. Modern detectors were not much better. This is why we are very excited to release Pangram Image Flash 1.0, a faster model that particularly excels at frontier AI video detection. On DF26 it scores 98.7%, a 29-point leap over the next best detector.

Industry Comparison

To compare against the industry, we took 129 real social media videos and generated AI mirrors using 14 different frontier video generators (100 videos each, sampled from the 129 real videos). The generators were each seeded with the first real frame from the input video and then prompted with a VLM-generated description of what happens in the video to make a difficult synthetic mirror. We then compared our model against multiple major AI video detection services across the 1,529 total videos:

An example of a real video (left) and its synthetic mirror (right). Could you tell which is real?

By starting from real video frames and creating a synthetic mirror, we can evaluate the model’s ability to distinguish between two very realistic looking videos. This prevents the model from introducing bias towards calling certain types of content AI, since each real video and its mirror share the same scene and subject.

Academic AI Video Detection Benchmarks

We compare our Image Flash model against several academic benchmarks for frontier AI video detection. We achieve state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks, which together include almost every frontier generation model for AI video.

Sources: AIGVDBench · DF26 · Ivy-Fake

Native Video Support

Pangram now natively supports video upload. Upload a video and Pangram Image Flash 1.0 will analyze it frame by frame to give you a complete analysis of which parts of the video come back as AI detected.

Chrome Extension

We have integrated Pangram Image 1.0 into our Chrome extension. This will flag AI-generated content while you scroll social media, online shopping, rental listings, and any other site where knowing that what you’re seeing is real matters.

API

With the release of Pangram Image 1.0 and Flash 1.0, we updated our API to support both image and video detection. We are excited to put the capability of these models into the hands of the community.

Isaac is a research engineer working on AI image/video detection at Pangram. He recently worked on 2D and 3D detection at Samsung AI Center NYC and has his Master’s in Robotics from the University of Minnesota.

item.title: Goodbye from Salon
item.description:
Today, after 31 years, we are saddened to announce that Salon is ceasing publication.

Itâs difficult to find the right words for the end of something that has meant so much to so many people. Salon was never just a website. It was an idea about what journalism could be, born at a moment when the internet was still a largely unexplored frontier.

When Salon launched in November 1995, the web was a very different place. A small group of journalists set out to create something original: a publication with a strong voice, a curiosity about the world and a belief that the internet could bring journalism and readers together in new ways. They helped pioneer a form of journalism that would come to define an entirely new era of publishing.

Over three decades, Salon has brought together politics, culture, criticism and ideas in a way that was distinctly our own. Our journalism examined power and politics, questioned assumptions, surfaced stories that deserved attention and made room for perspectives that were too often overlooked. Our writers and editors helped shape conversations about the forces changing our lives. The work was never simply about keeping up with the news. It was about making sense of it.

The history of Salon is also the history of the people who made it. We are profoundly grateful to the journalists, editors, photographers, producers, designers, business teams and countless other colleagues who brought this publication to life across its many chapters. To the founders who imagined it, the staff members who built it, the contributors who gave it their voices and the alumni who carried its spirit into the world: Thank you. Salon’s legacy belongs to all of you.

We also want to thank our readers. You came to Salon for the journalism, the dialogue, the essays, the criticism, the unexpected discoveries and the sense that there was a place on the internet where ideas mattered. You read, shared, challenged, subscribed, wrote to us and kept coming back. Your engagement made Salon a publication and a community, and it gave our work meaning. We are so grateful for the time you spent with us.

The business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years. After careful consideration, we have reached the difficult decision that our publishing model is no longer sustainable. We know this news will be deeply disappointing to many of you, and we share that sadness.

Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them. Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.

Thank you for being part of our story. It has been an extraordinary privilege.

Salon

item.title: The Cost of Blogging
item.description:
The Cost of Blogging

It’s easy enough to find a blogging platform that doesn’t cost anything to use, Bear itself has a decent enough free tier, but how many of us do end up spending some money on our little journals? For me, there’s a few things I always pay for:

A Personal Domain

When people buy a domain for their blog, it’s a clear sign they intend to stick around. I can become quite attached to a good blog, so I find myself more likely to follow someone with a domain because there’s a higher expectation they will continue it.

A domain is your online identity. If you own it, no one else can claim it. You can use it wherever you wish, and you can take it elsewhere if you’re not happy where you are. You won’t lose your readership because they follow the domain, not the platform.

For me, this is an essential expense.

The Blogging Platform / Hosting

In today’s age of data collection and privacy concerns, I prefer to pay for my blogging platform or hosting. Then I know that it’s my subscription and not my personal information that’s funding the development, server costs etc.

For smaller companies, like Bear, paying also helps support the free tier for those that don’t subscribe. Not everyone can afford to pay for their blog and I think it’s important to help keep that option alive, sustainably.

Typography

I’m undoubtably in the minority here as there are many wonderful free fonts available. However, as a typography nerd, I’m always looking for the next best thing and that means I’ve encountered some irresistible premium fonts. There is a ceiling on this - I have spent no more than £100 on a font family because that really is my justifiable limit for a personal blog.

I’ve written a few posts about the subject here:

I have actually changed the font again just yesterday, so the last post is not up-to-date

When I do use a free font, I always host it directly to avoid usage tracking (looking at you Google). I also try to use original font foundries, who sometimes sell premium fonts alongside their free offerings as a sustainable and ethical business model.

Writing Software

Bear includes a simple editor, but I much prefer to use something a little fuller-featured. There are plenty of text and markdown editors available for free, or for a nominal subscription - there’s no reason to spend a fortune, just pick the one that feels comfortable. I happen to like Paper, which is free with extra personalisation for an annual or lifetime cost. It has a very pleasant interface and allows me to use my own font. I blogged about it in Finding the Perfect Writing App.

What elements of blogging do you feel are worth paying for? If you happen to write a post about it, pop me a link and I’ll share.
